name: AI/ML track
duration: About 6 months at 8–10 hours a week
blurb: Python, the maths you actually need, classic machine learning, deep learning and shipping models. The foundation every AI job assumes.
start_if: Start here if you're new to coding or AI, or you want ML engineer or data scientist roles.

stages.title: Python and the everyday tools
stages.why: Every model, notebook and API you'll touch is Python. Get comfortable before anything else.

resources.title: CS50's Introduction to Programming with Python
resources.note: The clearest start if you've never coded.

resources.title: Kaggle Learn: Python
resources.note: Short lessons with exercises in the browser.

resources.title: NumPy: the absolute basics for beginners
Automate the Boring Stuff with Python
resources.note: Free to read online.

resources.title: GitHub Skills
resources.note: Learn Git by doing it in a real repo.

project.title: Explore a real dataset
project.text: Pick a dataset you care about (IPL matches, your city's weather, exam results from Kaggle). Clean it with Pandas, make 5 charts, write what you found, and push the notebook to GitHub.

done_when: You can write functions and a small class without looking things up
You can load, clean and group a CSV in Pandas
Your notebook is on GitHub with a readable README

stages.title: The maths you actually need
stages.why: Not a maths degree: just enough linear algebra, calculus and probability to understand what a model is doing.

resources.title: Essence of Linear Algebra
resources.note: Watch this first: pictures before formulas.

resources.title: StatQuest
resources.note: Short, friendly explanations of every stats and ML idea.

resources.title: Mathematics for Machine Learning
resources.note: Free PDF. Use as a reference, not cover to cover.

project.title: Gradient descent by hand
project.text: Implement linear regression with gradient descent in plain NumPy. Plot the loss going down, then try a learning rate that's too big and explain what happens.

done_when: You can explain a dot product and a gradient in your own words
You can say why we take small steps downhill to train a model
You know what mean, variance and a normal distribution are

stages.title: Classic machine learning
stages.why: Most real business problems are still solved with these models. They also teach you how to test any model honestly.
topics: Decision trees, random forests, gradient boosting

resources.title: Machine Learning Specialization
resources.note: Audit for free, or apply for Coursera financial aid for the certificate.

resources.title: Kaggle Learn: Intro to Machine Learning
resources.note: Then take Intermediate Machine Learning.

resources.title: Hands-On Machine Learning (3rd edition) notebooks
resources.note: The notebooks are free; the book itself is paid and worth it.

project.title: Two Kaggle problems, done properly
project.text: Solve Kaggle's Titanic (classification) and House Prices (regression). Use cross-validation, compare 3 models, and write down which features mattered and why.

done_when: You never judge a model on the data it trained on
You can choose a metric that fits the problem
You can explain why a random forest beat (or lost to) logistic regression

stages.title: Deep learning
stages.why: Neural networks power everything in the Gen AI track. Build one from scratch once, and nothing after feels like magic.
topics: Overfitting fixes: augmentation, dropout, weight decay

resources.title: Neural Networks: Zero to Hero
resources.note: Builds a neural network engine from scratch. The single best resource here.

resources.title: Practical Deep Learning for Coders
resources.note: Top-down and practical: working models from lesson one.

resources.title: Dive into Deep Learning
resources.note: Free interactive book with runnable code.

project.title: From micrograd to a real classifier
project.text: Follow Karpathy's micrograd lecture and build it yourself. Then train a CNN in PyTorch on a small image dataset you collect (for example, Indian dishes), first from scratch and then with transfer learning.

done_when: You can write a PyTorch training loop without copying it
You can explain backpropagation with a small example
You know how to spot and fix overfitting

stages.title: Vision and language
stages.why: Most AI products see images or read text. Learn the standard models and how to adapt them with Hugging Face.
topics: The Hugging Face Hub, Datasets and Transformers libraries

resources.title: CS231n: Deep Learning for Computer Vision
resources.note: Lectures and notes are free online.

resources.title: CS224n: Natural Language Processing with Deep Learning
LLM Course
resources.note: Transformers, tokenizers and fine-tuning, hands-on.

project.title: Fine-tune and publish
project.text: Fine-tune a pretrained model (a small vision transformer or DistilBERT) on your own dataset, then publish the model with a proper model card on the Hugging Face Hub.

done_when: You can load any model from the Hub and run it
You have fine-tuned a pretrained model on your own data
Your model is public with a model card

stages.title: Ship it: data, MLOps and deployment
stages.why: A model in a notebook helps nobody. Learn to serve it, version it and watch it once people use it.

resources.title: Made With ML
resources.note: Production ML end to end, written for engineers.

resources.title: MLOps Zoomcamp
resources.note: Free cohort course with homework and a community.

resources.title: Hugging Face Spaces
resources.note: Free hosting for demos.

resources.title: Modal
resources.note: Run heavy models on cloud GPUs by the second.

project.title: Put your model on the internet
project.text: Take your stage 4 or 5 model, wrap it in a FastAPI service inside Docker, add a Gradio demo on Hugging Face Spaces, and log every prediction so you can spot problems.

done_when: Anyone can try your model from a link
Your service runs the same on your laptop and in the cloud
You can tell when it starts getting worse

stages.title: Portfolio and interviews
stages.why: Turn what you built into proof. Recruiters look for finished projects you can explain, not certificates.

resources.title: Daily Papers
resources.note: The easiest way to follow new research.

project.title: Three projects you can explain
project.text: Polish three projects from this track: each with a clear README, a live demo link, what you tried that didn't work, and what you'd do next. Then enter one Kaggle competition.

done_when: Three projects with live demos and honest READMEs
You can walk an interviewer through one project's trade-offs in five minutes

name: Gen AI track
duration: About 4 months at 8–10 hours a week
blurb: How LLMs really work, then using them well: APIs, RAG, agents, evals, fine-tuning and shipping real AI products.
start_if: Start here if you know basic Python. Do AI/ML stages 1 to 4 first if you want to understand what's underneath.

stages.title: How LLMs actually work
stages.why: Before building with LLMs, know what they are: next-word predictors trained on huge amounts of text. It explains both their magic and their mistakes.

resources.title: Intro to Large Language Models
resources.note: One hour, the best overview there is.

resources.title: Deep Dive into LLMs like ChatGPT
resources.note: Longer and deeper: pre-training to reasoning models.

resources.title: Neural Networks (Transformer chapters)
resources.note: Beautiful visual explanations of attention.

resources.title: Tiktokenizer
resources.note: Type text and see exactly how a model splits it into tokens.

project.title: Explain it to a friend
project.text: Write a one-page explainer (with pictures) of how an LLM turns your question into an answer, token by token. Use Tiktokenizer to show real tokens.

done_when: You can explain tokens, embeddings and attention without jargon
You can say why an LLM confidently makes things up

stages.title: Use LLM APIs well
stages.why: Most Gen AI products are built on APIs. Learn prompting, structured outputs, streaming and costs properly.

resources.title: Google AI Studio
resources.note: A free Gemini API key: the easiest way to start without paying.

resources.title: Pydantic
resources.note: Validate the JSON a model gives you.

resources.title: Vercel AI SDK
resources.note: If you build in TypeScript.

project.title: A study helper that returns clean data
project.text: Build a command-line helper that turns a chapter of your notes into flashcards as validated JSON, streams the answer, retries on errors, and prints what each run cost.

done_when: Your app never crashes on a bad model reply
You get the same JSON shape every time
You know roughly what 1,000 requests would cost

stages.title: Build a small GPT from scratch
stages.why: Code the Transformer yourself once. After this, papers, model cards and fine-tuning all make sense.

resources.title: Let's build GPT: from scratch, in code
Build a Large Language Model (From Scratch)
resources.note: The code and videos are free; the book is paid.

resources.title: Attention Is All You Need
resources.note: The original Transformer paper. Read it after the videos.

project.title: Your own tiny GPT
project.text: Train a small GPT on text in your own language (Hindi, Tamil, Telugu…) or on your favourite author, on a free Colab GPU. Add temperature and top-k sampling and compare the outputs.

done_when: Your model generates text that looks like the training data
You can explain every line of your attention code

stages.title: RAG: answers from your own documents
stages.why: Models don't know your notes, PDFs or company data. RAG finds the right passages and hands them to the model, with citations.

resources.title: RAG From Scratch
resources.note: Short videos that build every RAG technique step by step.

resources.title: Advanced RAG on Hugging Face documentation
Sentence Transformers
resources.note: Free, local embedding models.

resources.title: pgvector
resources.note: Vector search inside PostgreSQL.

resources.title: Docling
resources.note: Turn PDFs into clean text and tables.

resources.title: Ragas
resources.note: Metrics for RAG quality.

project.title: A study assistant for your notes
project.text: Build a chat app over your own college notes and PDFs that cites the page for every answer and says “I don't know” when the notes don't cover it. (This is the Build Challenge project.)

done_when: Every answer shows where it came from
It refuses to guess when the answer isn't in your documents
You have 20 test questions with expected answers

stages.title: Agents and MCP
stages.why: Agents let a model take steps: call tools, read results and decide what's next. Learn to build ones that don't break.
topics: The agent loop: reason, act, observe

resources.title: Building effective agents
resources.note: Read this before any framework.

resources.title: Model Context Protocol
resources.note: The standard way to plug tools and data into AI apps.

project.title: An agent that asks before it acts
project.text: Build an agent that plans your study week from your notes and calendar through MCP, stops for your approval before changing anything, and has a hard limit on steps and cost.

done_when: Your agent stops and asks when it isn't sure
It can't loop forever or spend without limit
You can replay every step it took

stages.title: Evals, safety and security
stages.why: You can't improve what you don't measure, and every AI app can be attacked. Test before your users do.

resources.title: Promptfoo
resources.note: Automated tests and red-teaming.

resources.title: Arize Phoenix
resources.note: See every step your app took, locally.

project.title: Break your own app
project.text: Write 30 test cases for your RAG app and 10 attack prompts (for example, a PDF that says “ignore your instructions”). Run them on every change and fix what fails.

done_when: You run your evals with one command
You know your app's weakest spot and have a fix for it

stages.title: Fine-tuning and open models
stages.why: Sometimes prompting isn't enough. Learn when to fine-tune, and how to do it cheaply on a free GPU.
topics: When to fine-tune vs prompt vs RAG

resources.title: Unsloth documentation and free notebooks
resources.note: Fine-tune on a free Colab GPU.

resources.title: Ollama
resources.note: Run open models on your own laptop.

resources.title: DeepSeek-R1 paper
resources.note: How reasoning models are trained with reinforcement learning.

project.title: Beat the prompt
project.text: Fine-tune a small open model (1–3B parameters) with QLoRA on a narrow task, such as turning messy notes into your college's exam format. Compare it with plain prompting, then run it locally with Ollama.

done_when: You can say when fine-tuning is worth it and when it isn't
Your fine-tuned model beats the base model on your test set

stages.title: Images, audio and multimodal
stages.why: Text is only one kind of generation. See how image, speech and vision-language models work, and where GANs and VAEs came from.

resources.title: Whisper
resources.note: Open speech-to-text you can run yourself.

resources.title: DCGAN tutorial
resources.note: Build a GAN once to see how generation started.

project.title: Lecture to notes
project.text: Build a demo that turns a recorded lecture into notes with Whisper, then generates a diagram for one key idea with a diffusion model. Host it on Hugging Face Spaces.

done_when: You can explain how diffusion turns noise into an image
Your demo works on a real recording

stages.title: Ship a real AI product
stages.why: Put it in front of real users: logins, limits, costs, speed and monitoring. This is what makes a project production-ready.

resources.title: AI Engineering
resources.note: The best single book on building AI products.

resources.title: Supabase
resources.note: Database, login and storage for your app.

resources.title: LMArena
resources.note: Compare models on real prompts.

resources.title: Artificial Analysis
resources.note: Speed and price of every model.

project.title: Launch it
project.text: Deploy your RAG or agent app for real users with login, rate limits, a cost dashboard and your evals running on every change. Get 10 people to use it and fix what they hit.

done_when: Real people use your app from a link
You know your cost per user and your slowest step
Your evals run before every deploy
